title: Foreign Research
description: The foreign research exclusion, IRC § 41(d)(4)(F), bars the R&D credit for research conducted outside the United States, Puerto Rico or U.S. possessions.
summary: The foreign research exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(F) bars taxpayers from claiming the federal R&D tax credit for research physically conducted outside the United States, Puerto Rico, or U.S. possessions. Wages, supplies, and contract costs for offshore work are 100% disallowed, regardless of headquarters or IP ownership, and post-TCJA Section 174 requires 15-year amortization of foreign research expenditures.

body.text: The foreign research exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(F) bars taxpayers from claiming the federal R&D tax credit for research physically conducted outside the United States, Puerto Rico, or U.S. possessions. Wages, supplies, and contract costs for offshore work are 100% disallowed, regardless of headquarters or IP ownership, and post-TCJA Section 174 requires 15-year amortization of foreign research expenditures.
Statutory Foundation and the Bright-Line Geographic Exclusion

For purposes of the federal Research and Development (R&D) Tax Credit under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41, the tax treatment of cross-border innovation is governed by an absolute statutory boundary. Originally enacted in the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 to stimulate technological investment, scientific experimentation, and high-skilled technical employment exclusively within the domestic economy, the credit enforces its territorial mandate through the explicit "Foreign Research" exclusion codified at 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(F). Under this provision, the statutory definition of "qualified research" categorically excludes any research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any possession of the United States.

Unlike international tax provisions that rely on subjective facts-and-circumstances balancing tests or permit proportional apportionment based on corporate nexus, sales footprint, or intangible asset ownership, IRC § 41(d)(4)(F) establishes a rigid, bright-line geographical test. Eligibility for Qualified Research Expenses (QREs)—which encompass in-house employee wages under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i), tangible research supplies under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii), and third-party contract research costs under IRC § 41(b)(3)—depends strictly on the physical situs where the hands-on scientific or technological experimentation takes place. Zero percent of wages, supply expenditures, or contractor payments attributable to research activities physically performed outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or U.S. possessions can be included in the QRE calculation.

This territorial boundary operates independently of corporate ownership, intellectual property (IP) domicile, payment origin, employee nationality, or the ultimate commercial destination of the resulting product. Research physically conducted outside the specified U.S. jurisdictions is statutorily disqualified regardless of whether the project is directed by executives at a U.S. corporate headquarters, funded directly by a domestic parent entity from a U.S. bank account, performed by U.S. citizens traveling temporarily abroad, or engineered to produce intellectual property legally registered, held, and commercialized exclusively within the United States. Conversely, the geographic test does not discriminate based on the nationality of the taxpayer's parent organization. Foreign-owned U.S. subsidiaries are fully permitted to claim the IRC § 41 credit to the extent their qualified research activities are physically performed within the United States and satisfy all other statutory prerequisites, including the substantive requirements against funded research under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H).

The interaction between the geographic exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(F) and the broader corporate tax architecture creates an asymmetric compliance landscape in which the physical location of individual engineers dictates both immediate credit eligibility and long-term cost recovery. The table below synthesizes the primary statutory and operational distinctions between domestic and foreign research activities under federal tax law.

body.text: The Physical Presence Standard and Mechanics of Conducted Research

Applying the IRC § 41(d)(4)(F) exclusion requires a granular legal and operational determination of where research is "conducted". Within the statutory architecture of IRC § 41(d), underlying technical activities must first satisfy the foundational four-part test before the geographic test determines whether the associated expenditures enter the QRE base. First, the activity must satisfy the Permitted Purpose test, meaning it is intended to develop a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality of a business component. Second, the activity must pursue the Elimination of Uncertainty, addressing technical uncertainty regarding capability, method, or appropriate design. Third, the investigation must be Technological in Nature, relying fundamentally on principles of the hard sciences—such as physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science—in accordance with IRC § 174 principles. Fourth, the taxpayer must engage in a Process of Experimentation, evaluating technical alternatives through systematic trial and error, modeling, or simulation.

Once an activity clears these four substantive thresholds, the physical presence standard governs geographic eligibility. Under this standard, the legal situs of research is defined strictly as the exact geographic location of the personnel executing the experimental work during the specific hours claimed. Because modern R&D workflows frequently span multiple sovereign jurisdictions through cloud infrastructure, collaborative version-control repositories, and globally integrated engineering teams, isolating the physical location of the human actor performing each discrete task is the cornerstone of IRC § 41 compliance.
In-House Wages, Employee Mobility, and Supervisory Boundaries

For in-house employee wages—which typically constitute the single largest component of a corporate taxpayer's QRE base—qualification centers on the performance of "qualified services" as defined in IRC § 41(b)(2)(B). In auditing wage claims, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) Audit Techniques Guide (ATG) emphasizes that "eligibility is based solely upon what an employee actually does, or does not, do during a specific time period," rather than relying on formal job titles, organizational chart placements, or generalized position descriptions. When applied in conjunction with the IRC § 41(d)(4)(F) geographic exclusion, this time-specific activity standard creates rigorous compliance obligations for internationally mobile employees.

If a U.S.-based scientist, software developer, or engineer temporarily travels outside the United States to perform experimental testing, prototype integration, or clinical evaluation, the wages earned during the foreign stay are categorically disqualified under IRC § 41(d)(4)(F). This disqualification applies even though the employee remains continuously on the U.S. corporate payroll and works uninterruptedly toward resolving the exact same technological uncertainty initiated in the domestic laboratory. Consider the hypothetical compliance scenario involving ManuCorp, a U.S. manufacturing corporation developing an improved industrial production process. If a U.S.-based chemical engineer whose primary duties involve qualified research at ManuCorp's domestic laboratory travels to a foreign affiliate's manufacturing facility in Mexico for a one-month period to execute specialized testing, ManuCorp must isolate that one-month foreign window from the engineer's annual payroll record. Both the wages paid to the chemical engineer for the hours physically worked in Mexico and all associated international travel expenses are excluded from the IRC § 41 credit calculation because the physical act of experimentation occurred outside qualified U.S. territory.

A nuanced legal boundary governs technical supervision and management across international borders. Under IRC § 41(d)(4)(D), activities related to general management functions, efficiency surveys, or market research are statutorily excluded from qualified research. However, direct first-line supervision or direct support of technical R&D work performed by technical managers can qualify as eligible services under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B), potentially allowing full wage inclusion if the supervisor satisfies the "substantially all" threshold within the United States. When cross-border engineering operations are involved, this rule bifurcates along strict geographic and substantive lines depending on whether the manager travels abroad or directs offshore teams remotely from the United States. Where a U.S. technical executive spends the majority of their time overseeing domestic technical teams in the United States, those supervisory wages are eligible; however, if that executive travels internationally to supervise foreign researchers on-site at an offshore laboratory, the wages corresponding to the time physically spent abroad are disqualified under the geographical exclusion.

Conversely, if a technical leader remains physically inside the United States while designing system specifications and reviewing work executed by a foreign engineering team, the two labor pools must be strictly decoupled on a substance-over-form basis. In the hypothetical "Remote Team" Scenario, a Senior Software Architect physically located in Austin, Texas designs core system architecture, drafts technical specifications, and conducts experimental code reviews, while a team of software developers located in Bangalore, India—employed by the U.S. company's foreign subsidiary—writes the underlying source code. Because the Austin-based Architect's physical activities take place entirely within the United States and constitute direct participation in resolving technological uncertainty through architectural design and code validation, 100% of the Architect's qualified wages are eligible QREs. In contrast, 100% of the wages and supply costs incurred by the Bangalore development team are excluded as Foreign Research under IRC § 41(d)(4)(F). This bifurcation demonstrates an essential statutory principle: technical direction or supervision originating from the United States never converts foreign labor into qualified domestic expenditure, nor does the offshore execution of coding tasks taint the domestic hands-on architectural engineering performed inside the United States.
Third-Party Contract Research Across Jurisdictions

The physical presence mandate applies with equal force to third-party contract research expenses governed by IRC § 41(b)(3). When a U.S. taxpayer engages an external vendor or independent research institution to conduct systematic trial-and-error testing, only the portion of the contracted work physically performed within the United States, Puerto Rico, or a U.S. possession is eligible for inclusion in QREs.

Returning to the hypothetical ManuCorp illustration, if ManuCorp contracts with a third-party engineering firm located in Germany to perform systematic testing to eliminate technical uncertainty in its manufacturing process, 100% of the payments attributable to the German contractor's offshore execution are disqualified as Foreign Research. The fact that the contract is funded by a domestic corporation and vests all resulting intellectual property rights in ManuCorp's U.S. entity does not alter the geographic disqualification. Furthermore, where a global vendor with multi-jurisdictional operations performs part of a project domestically—such as initial project planning in a U.S. facility—and shifts another portion offshore—such as foreign execution and testing—the taxpayer cannot treat the contract as a unified domestic expense. Instead, the taxpayer must obtain granular invoice breakdowns segregating U.S. hours and domestic costs from non-U.S. hours and offshore costs, excluding the foreign tranche entirely.
Financial Ramifications: The Dual Penalty of Credit Forfeiture and Section 174 Amortization

Misclassifying domestic versus offshore research or strategically shifting R&D activities outside the United States triggers a severe, two-fold financial penalty under the Internal Revenue Code. Rather than merely losing a marginal tax incentive, corporations conducting foreign research experience a compounded deterioration in both their effective tax rate and their multi-year operating cash flows.

The first penalty is the immediate and permanent forfeiture of the IRC § 41 tax credit on all offshore expenditures. Under the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) method codified at IRC § 41(c)(4)(A), the research credit provides a direct dollar-for-dollar reduction in federal income tax liability equal to up to 14% of incremental qualified research expenditures. Forfeiting this credit on offshore engineering outlays directly reduces the immediate after-tax return on innovation investment compared to domestic research.

The second—and frequently more punishing—financial consequence arises under IRC § 174, as amended by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) for tax years beginning after December 31, 2021. Under the post-TCJA IRC § 174 regime, taxpayers are prohibited from immediately deducting Research and Experimental (R&E) expenditures in the taxable year incurred and must instead capitalize and amortize those costs. Crucially, the statute imposes a steeply asymmetric recovery schedule based strictly on where the research is conducted: domestic R&E expenditures must be capitalized and amortized ratably over a 5-year period (60 months), whereas Foreign Research Expenditures (FREs) must be capitalized and amortized over a mandatory 15-year period (180 months). While taxpayers evaluating current-year versus prior-year returns must always verify the effective dates of any subsequent statutory amendments to IRC § 174, the post-TCJA framework effective for tax years beginning after December 31, 2021 establishes this stark 5-year domestic versus 15-year foreign amortization divide.
Hypothetical Worked Calculation: Quantifying the Dual Penalty

To illustrate the combined quantitative mechanics of the IRC § 41(d)(4)(F) exclusion and the post-TCJA IRC § 174 capitalization regime, consider a hypothetical U.S. corporation modeled with an annual Domestic R&D Spend of $500,000 and an annual Foreign R&D Spend of $250,000:
Domestic R&D Spend = $500,000
Foreign R&D Spend = $250,000
Combining the domestic and offshore outlays yields a Total Worldwide R&D Spend of $750,000:
Total Worldwide R&D Spend = $500,000 + $250,000 = $750,000
Under the first step of the compliance computation—determining the IRC § 41 QRE Base—100% of the $250,000 Foreign R&D Spend is statutorily disqualified under IRC § 41(d)(4)(F):
Lost QRE Base (Disallowed Foreign Research) = $250,000 × 100% = $250,000
Net Eligible QRE Base = $750,000 − $250,000 = $500,000

Consequently, for any incremental research expenditures exceeding the statutory base amount, the maximum 14% Alternative Simplified Credit rate applies solely to the $500,000 domestic pool. Even if the entire $250,000 foreign expenditure would otherwise have represented incremental QREs, applying the maximum 14% ASC rate demonstrates that the geographic exclusion permanently forfeits up to $35,000 in potential federal tax credit value:
Maximum Forfeited ASC Value on Foreign Tranche = $250,000 × 14% = $35,000

Under the second step of the computation—evaluating the post-TCJA IRC § 174 annual amortization disparity—the mandatory 60-month domestic recovery period yields a 20% deduction per full 12-month amortization year (12/60 = 20%), whereas the 180-month foreign recovery period yields only 6.67% per full 12-month amortization year (12/180 ≈ 6.67%):
Annual Domestic Amortization (Full Year) = $500,000 / 5 years = $100,000 per year (20.00%)
Annual Foreign Amortization (Full Year) = $250,000 / 15 years = $16,666.67 per year (6.67%)

Had that $250,000 foreign tranche instead been performed physically inside the United States (recovering over 5 years at $250,000 / 5 = $50,000 per full year), the corporation would have realized an additional $33,333.33 ($50,000 − $16,666.67) in annual tax deductions during each full year of the primary 5-year recovery window. By tripling the amortization horizon from 60 months to 180 months, IRC § 174 severely erodes the Net Present Value (NPV) of the tax deduction and imposes an acute cash-flow drag on offshore R&D. body.text: Advanced Multinational Enterprise (MNE) Nexus and Cross-Border Interactions

For multinational enterprises (MNEs), the IRC § 41(d)(4)(F) geographic exclusion does not operate in isolation; it intersects directly with three complex international tax regimes governing intercompany risk allocation, cross-border expense apportionment, and intangible income deductions. Navigating these overlapping rules requires coordinating domestic R&D tax credit studies with international transfer pricing and foreign tax credit modeling.
The Funded Research Exclusion (IRC § 41(d)(4)(H)) for Foreign-Owned U.S. Subsidiaries

While a foreign-owned U.S. subsidiary satisfies the geographic situs test of IRC § 41(d)(4)(F) when its engineers physically conduct research inside the United States, its claim frequently confronts a second, independent statutory hurdle: the "Funded Research" exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H). This provision disqualifies research from the IRC § 41 credit to the extent it is "funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person".

When a U.S. subsidiary performs R&D under an intercompany service agreement with its foreign parent or an offshore principal company, IRS examiners scrutinize the underlying legal contracts to determine whether the domestic research is "funded". Under controlling Treasury Regulations—specifically Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)—the legal requirement for avoiding the funded research exclusion is strictly conjunctive rather than disjunctive. To claim the IRC § 41 credit for research performed on behalf of another party, the taxpayer performing the research must both bear the financial risk of failure—meaning that payment to the U.S. subsidiary is contingent upon successful research results rather than guaranteed on a cost-plus basis—and retain substantial rights in the resulting intellectual property or research output.

If a foreign-owned U.S. subsidiary operates as a routine, low-risk contract R&D service provider that is compensated by its foreign parent on a guaranteed cost-plus markup while transferring all IP rights exclusively to the foreign parent, the research fails this regulatory test. Because the U.S. subsidiary does not both bear the financial risk of failure and retain substantial rights in the results, the research is deemed "funded" under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and is excluded from the IRC § 41 credit despite being physically performed in the United States. Consequently, foreign-owned U.S. subsidiaries must align their intercompany agreements and transfer pricing studies to substantiate both domestic physical performance and genuine economic risk and IP rights retention.
Expense Allocation, Apportionment, and the Foreign Tax Credit Limitation (IRC §§ 861–862)

The classification and geographic location of R&D expenditures also directly impact a U.S. multinational corporation's Foreign Tax Credit (FTC) limitation. Under IRC §§ 861 and 862 (and the implementing regulations under Treasury Regulation § 1.861-8), U.S. corporations must allocate and apportion deductions—including R&E expenditures—between domestic-source income and foreign-source income. When R&D expenditures cannot be definitely allocated to a single income class, a statutory portion must be apportioned against foreign-source gross income.

This mandatory apportionment creates significant international tax friction. Apportioning a U.S. corporation's domestic R&D deductions against its foreign-source income reduces net foreign-source taxable income, which in turn reduces the maximum Foreign Tax Credit the corporation can claim. As analyzed in Treasury Office of Tax Analysis (OTA) Paper 43, this regulation has historically proved controversial and punitive for MNEs in an excess FTC position because foreign tax authorities generally do not permit a local tax deduction for R&D expenses physically performed in the United States. By mandatorily assigning a portion of a U.S. corporation's domestic R&D expenses against foreign-source income without a corresponding foreign tax deduction abroad, the apportionment rules can effectively deny any tax benefit for that portion, raising the MNE's worldwide effective tax rate.
Strategic Tension and Synergy with Foreign-Derived Intangible Income (FDII)

In contrast to the friction caused by IRC § 861 expense apportionment, the interplay between the IRC § 41 credit and the Foreign-Derived Intangible Income (FDII) deduction provides a compelling strategic incentive for MNEs to centralize R&D operations physically within the United States. FDII is designed to reduce the effective U.S. corporate tax rate on income derived from intangible property or services sold or provided to foreign persons for foreign use.

Recent administrative guidance in Private Letter Ruling (PLR) 202502002 concluded that service fee income earned by a U.S. entity for providing R&D services to a related foreign operating company may be characterized entirely as Foreign-Derived Deduction Eligible Income (FDDEI). Although Private Letter Rulings are not binding precedent, PLR 202502002 illustrates the structural potential for a dual tax benefit: R&D physically performed inside the United States clears the IRC § 41(d)(4)(F) geographical test, while the service fee income generated from providing that research to a foreign affiliate may simultaneously qualify for the FDII deduction. Realizing this dual benefit requires advanced transfer pricing analysis under the IRC § 482 controlled service transaction regulations to substantiate the arm's-length nature of the intercompany service charges, alongside careful contract structuring so that the intercompany arrangement does not trigger the IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) funded research exclusion.
Operational Compliance, Cost Segregation, and IRS Audit Preparedness

Because the geographic exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(F) operates as an absolute bar to credit eligibility, IRS examiners treat cross-border cost segregation as a primary audit focus area. When auditing the research credit, examiners rely on contemporaneous records—including payroll registers, employee job descriptions, performance evaluations, calendars, and appointment books—to verify the exact hours worked within the United States. Failure by a taxpayer to provide clear, contemporaneous evidence separating domestic costs from foreign costs risks the disallowance of the entire domestic QRE base under examination.

To establish a defensible audit posture, multinational taxpayers must implement rigorous internal controls across three operational verification protocols: third-party contract review, employee time-tracking segmentation, and substance-over-form supervisory isolation. Under the contract review protocol, taxpayers must examine all third-party vendor agreements and ensure that Statements of Work (SOWs) specify that research must be performed within the United States; if a vendor operates globally, the taxpayer must request an itemized breakdown of U.S. versus non-U.S. hours on every invoice. Under the time-tracking segmentation protocol, organizations must update electronic time-tracking systems to include a geographic location code whenever U.S. employees travel internationally or work remotely from abroad, isolating disqualified foreign travel hours from eligible domestic hours. Finally, under the substance-over-form analysis, taxpayers must isolate a U.S. manager's domestic direction and review time (which is qualified) from an offshore team's execution time (which is excluded), rather than aggregating both labor pools into a single undifferentiated "Development" cost center. body.text: Conclusions and Strategic Recommendations for Regulatory and Legislative Clarity

The Foreign Research exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(F) enforces Congress's intent to anchor technological innovation and high-skilled R&D employment physically within the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, and U.S. possessions. By coupling complete QRE disqualification under IRC § 41 with the mandatory 15-year (180-month) amortization period for Foreign Research Expenditures under post-TCJA IRC § 174, the federal tax code imposes a substantial financial penalty on offshore experimentation. For multinational enterprises, rigorous operational cost segregation and proactive structural planning around the IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) Funded Research exclusion, IRC § 861 expense apportionment, and the FDII regime are essential compliance imperatives.

To resolve emerging ambiguities in modern cross-border R&D workflows and improve the efficiency of the domestic innovation incentive framework, three targeted administrative and legislative actions are warranted. First, the IRS and the Treasury Department should issue formal public guidance applying the "physical presence" test to distributed digital R&D activities—such as cloud computing environments, remote-access software development, and globally dispersed machine learning model training—clarifying how strategic planning or core experimental data processing conducted in the United States qualifies when user interfaces or execution nodes span multiple jurisdictions. Second, policymakers should elevate the analytical principles of PLR 202502002 into proposed and final regulations, providing binding precedent on the qualification of intercompany R&D service income as FDDEI and clarifying the exact interplay between IRC § 41, FDII, and the IRC § 482 controlled service transaction regulations. Third, Congress should enact legislative reform to reduce the punitive 15-year (180-month) amortization period for Foreign Research Expenditures under IRC § 174; because IRC § 41(d)(4)(F) already denies the tax credit for foreign research, moderating the 15-year amortization schedule would alleviate disproportionate cash-flow burdens on global R&D operations while preserving the IRC § 41 credit exclusively for domestic research.
